Caddish describes behavior that is dishonorable, selfish, and deeply ungentlemanly — especially the way a person (almost always a man) treats others, particularly women, in a way that is unfair, dishonest, or morally cheap.

If someone acts in a caddish way, they know what decent, respectful behavior looks like — but they deliberately choose not to follow it, usually because they are putting their own selfish interests above someone else's feelings, dignity, or well-being.

The key to understanding this word is this: a caddish person is not simply rude or thoughtless. Rudeness can happen by accident. Caddish behavior is more specific — it involves a knowing betrayal of decency, a willingness to treat people in ways that are beneath acceptable standards of honor and integrity.

Think of it as a specific flavor of bad character. It sits somewhere between "merely impolite" and "outright villainous." A cad isn't a monster — but he is someone you simply cannot trust or respect.
The Most Common Situations Where This Word Is Used

1. In relationships and romance
This is the most classic use of the word. A caddish man might pursue a woman, make her feel special, gain her trust and affection — and then abandon her without any sense of guilt or responsibility. He might make promises he never intends to keep, flirt without any sincerity, or use someone emotionally and then discard them.

2. In friendships and social trust
Caddish behavior also shows up when someone takes advantage of a friend's kindness — for example, borrowing money and never repaying it while making excuses, or revealing a friend's private secret for personal gain.

3. In professional or competitive settings
Taking credit for someone else's hard work, cheating when no one is looking, or using your position of power to exploit someone weaker than you — these are all caddish acts.
The Key Traits That Make Something "Caddish"

• Selfishness — the caddish person prioritizes their own comfort, pleasure, or gain over another person's feelings or dignity.
  • Dishonesty or insincerity — they are not straight with people; they mislead, charm falsely, or give the impression of something they don't mean.
  • A betrayal of trust — caddish behavior often involves someone who was trusted and who broke that trust in a mean-spirited or cowardly way.
  • Knowing better but not caring — this is crucial. A caddish person is not naive or ignorant. They know the decent thing to do. They just don't do it.
  • Cowardice — a cad often takes the easy, selfish path and avoids facing the consequences of their actions honestly.

• It is not just "being rude." You can be rude by accident or out of nervousness. Caddish behavior has a deliberate, self-serving quality to it.
  • It is not the same as being violent or criminal. A cad operates within social situations — he hurts people emotionally and morally, not physically.
  • It is not a casual or light insult. Calling someone's behavior caddish is a serious moral judgment about their character.
The Tone and Feel of the Word

This word carries a somewhat old-fashioned, British flavor. It comes from a world where concepts like being a gentleman, acting with honor, and treating others with dignity were taken very seriously. Because of this, the word has a slightly formal, literary feel — you are more likely to read it in a novel or a sharp opinion piece than hear it in everyday street conversation. However, it is absolutely still used today, and when it is used, it lands with real weight. It tells you not just that someone behaved badly, but that their behavior revealed something cheap and dishonorable about their character.

• "It was caddish of him to tell everyone about her personal struggles the moment they broke up."
  • "He had a caddish habit of charming women into trusting him, then disappearing without a word."
  • "Taking all the credit for the team's work was, frankly, a caddish thing to do."
  • "She had always suspected there was something caddish beneath his polished manners."

Caddish describes the behavior of someone who knows how a decent, honorable person acts — but who selfishly, dishonestly, and cowardly chooses to treat others in ways that fall far below that standard, especially in personal relationships and matters of trust.
